Footer.source: Source: TF.js COCO-SSD (Google); Z-AI Web Dev SDK; internal simulation on Pexels/Pixabay stock footage of Peru plaza scenes.

hero.title: An agentic camera intelligence system that converts Peru's public plaza feeds into automated, auditable incident response — running entirely in the browser.
hero.body: The system pairs a traditional computer-vision layer (TF.js COCO-SSD, 90-class object detection) with an agentic reasoning layer (rule engine + LLM-as-judge) that perceives, decides, and acts on anomalies in real time — without sending camera frames to a remote server.

scr.situationBody: Peru's public plazas (Cusco, Lima, Arequipa) are monitored by ad-hoc camera feeds. Operators watch screens manually, react late, and rarely produce an auditable incident trail.
scr.complicationBody: Manual monitoring means 10–15 min mean-time-to-respond, high false-alarm fatigue, no snapshot evidence at the moment of incident, and zero searchable history.
scr.resolutionBody: An in-browser agentic loop: COCO-SSD perceives → rule engine reasons → 3-tier escalation acts → snapshot+report logged. Under 2 seconds per cycle, with full evidence trail.

bigNumber.title: Experimental local-first browser workflow; performance varies by device, backend, source, and selected model.
bigNumber.body: Latency budget breakdown: TF.js COCO-SSD inference ≈ 250–500 ms on a mid-tier laptop GPU · rule-engine reasoning < 5 ms · action dispatch (snapshot, email sim, optional LLM judge) ≈ 200–800 ms. The remaining budget is canvas redraw and React state propagation. All numbers measured on the live prototype.
bigNumber.source: Source: internal measurement on MacBook Pro M2, 2026-07-14. Manual review baseline: industry typical 8–15 min MTTR for unmonitored CCTV.

architecture.title: Five-stage pipeline turns raw video frames into escalated, evidence-backed incidents — each stage adding a layer of intelligence.
architecture.stage1Desc: Captures each video frame, runs the 90-class object-detection model in-browser, and emits bounding boxes + confidence scores. Pure perception — no decisions.
architecture.stage2Desc: Maintains a 2-minute sliding window of person counts. Computes mean, stddev, z-score, and EMA control-chart residual — pure statistics, no decisions.
architecture.stage3Desc: Consumes the anomaly score + sustain counter + escalation history. Decides whether to escalate, hold, or stand down. Optionally invokes the LLM-as-judge to filter false positives.
architecture.stage4Desc: Executes the decided actions: log_hit, snapshot, send_email, generate_report, escalate. Each action is observable in the audit trail with timestamp + payload.
architecture.stage5Desc: On Tier ≥ 2, freezes a JPEG snapshot with bounding boxes overlaid. On Tier 3, auto-generates a corporate incident report. Operators can acknowledge or silence to tune thresholds.
architecture.layerIAItem1: YOLO/COCO-SSD object detection — no decisions, just bounding boxes
architecture.layerAgenticItem1: Rule registry: data-driven thresholds (z>2, z>2.5 sustained 3 ticks, z>3.5 → Tier 3)
architecture.layerAgenticItem2: LLM-as-judge: optional false-positive filter on snapshot
architecture.layerAgenticItem4: Action audit trail + snapshot + auto-generated incident report

pillars.title: Three capabilities differentiate the system from passive surveillance: real-time perception, agentic reasoning, and automated escalation.
pillars.pillar1Body: TensorFlow.js + COCO-SSD runs the same 90-class object detection model used by production CV systems, but client-side. No GPU server, no frame leaves the browser — addresses both latency and privacy at once.
pillars.pillar2Body: A deterministic evidence policy owns authority. An optional authenticated judge is advisory and runs before action proposal; no false-positive reduction rate has been validated.
pillars.pillar3Body: A tool registry executes auditable actions: badge → snapshot+email → escalate+report. A human-acknowledge gate and a max-5/hour circuit breaker prevent alert fatigue and runaway automation.
pillars.pillar3Metric: Local actions only on GitHub Pages

roadmap.title: v1 ships the core agentic loop; v2 adds visual memory for similar-incident lookup; v3 scales to a multi-camera mesh.
roadmap.v2Item3: Operator feedback loop tunes judge prompt
roadmap.risk1: Model drift. COCO-SSD trained on general images; Peru plaza footage may need fine-tuning for distant/small persons.
roadmap.risk2: Browser performance varies substantially; WebGPU absence, WASM fallback, memory, and decode limits must be measured per device.
roadmap.risk3: Privacy compliance. Snapshots store identifiable images — need retention policy + on-prem option for production.

privacy.title: All processing runs in the operator's browser — no camera frames leave the device, and snapshots stay local until explicitly escalated.
privacy.card1Body: TensorFlow.js runs entirely client-side. The video element, the canvas pixel buffer, and the detection tensors never touch a server. The only network calls are the optional LLM-judge and email endpoints, which receive only telemetry JSON — not raw frames.
privacy.card2Body: Evidence may be stored in IndexedDB when available. Browser storage is best-effort, user-deletable, and subject to eviction; the UI exposes deletion and retention status.
privacy.card3Body: Actions record timestamps and outcomes for review. Browser logs are not immutable and must not be treated as a tamper-proof chain of custody.

help.title: How to use the prototype
help.step1: Pick a camera feed (urban traffic with real people and vehicles).
help.step2: Click Start analysis — the AI model (COCO-SSD) loads in your browser (~5s first time) then detects people and vehicles in real time.
help.step3: Watch the chart fill in. After ~10 seconds the system learns the normal pattern; unusual activity will trigger alerts (Tier 1=watch, 2=anomaly, 3=critical).
help.step4: Use the sliders in Agent reasoning to adjust sensitivity. Toggle the LLM judge to filter false positives. Switch capability levels to see how the system behavior changes.
help.step5: Review alerts and local tracks. Track IDs reset with the source and never establish identity.

slide1.title: AI has crossed four thresholds in 70 years — and the fourth, agentic systems, is the one that finally acts on the world.
slide1.body: Since the 1956 Dartmouth Workshop, artificial intelligence has progressed through four capability eras: rule-based programs, machine learning, generative AI, and now agentic systems. Each era automated a slice of work but stopped at the screen. The leap to agentic AI closes the loop — systems now perceive, reason, act, and self-correct against goals.
slide1.situationBody: Four AI eras in 70 years. Each solved the previous era's ceiling but stopped short of action.
slide1.complicationBody: Gartner: AI agents are the fastest-advancing tech on the 2025 Hype Cycle. 60% of orgs expect to deploy within 2 years.
slide1.resolutionBody: Vision Agent is built natively on the agentic pattern: perceive → reason → act → reflect, end to end.

slide2.title: Each AI era solved the previous era's ceiling — rules lacked learning, learning lacked generation, generation lacked action.
slide2.body: The four eras are not strictly sequential — they are nested capabilities. Every Stage 4 agentic system contains Stage 3 generative models that were trained using Stage 2 deep learning on patterns originally identified by Stage 1 rules. Each era ADDED a capability without losing the previous one.
slide2.timelineEnd: 2025 — Agentic AI at Peak of Expectations

slide3.title: Four stages, nested not sequential — every agentic system still contains rules, learning, and generative models inside it.
slide3.body: This is the dense reference card for the rest of the brief. Each card defines what the era IS, what it CAN do, what it CAN'T do, and the economic value it created. The nesting insight (bottom-right) is critical: agentic AI does not replace generative AI — it builds on top of it. Use cases evolve from simple counting (Stage 1) through perception tasks like graffiti and fire detection (Stage 2), content generation for incident reports (Stage 3), to end-to-end autonomous response including auto-generated reports and LLM-judged escalation (Stage 4).
slide3.nestingTitle: The nesting insight — capabilities stack, they don't replace
slide3.nestingBody: An effective Stage 4 system (agentic) almost always contains Stage 3 agents that use Stage 2 generative models that were trained on patterns originally identified by Stage 1 systems. Removing any layer breaks the whole stack.

slide4.title: Agentic AI adds the loop the previous eras lacked: perceive, reason, act, reflect — and repeat until the goal is met.
slide4.body: Generative AI does input → output. Agentic AI does input → plan → act → verify → revise. The loop is the whole point. It is what lets an agent pursue a goal over time, recover from failure, and adapt to changing conditions — capabilities no prior era had.

slide5.title: Generative AI produces output; agentic AI pursues goals — the difference is tool use, multi-step planning, and self-correction.
slide5.body: For skeptical executives who think "agentic" is just a rebrand of generative AI. The matrix below makes the distinction concrete across six capability dimensions. The right column is not a bigger version of the left — it is a different category of system.
slide5.bottomLineBody: Generative AI gave us copilots that assist human work by generating output. Agentic AI can reason, collaborate, and coordinate multistep work across systems. The shift is from assistance to execution.

slide6.title: True agency begins only at Level 5 — when the system can loop, retry, and self-correct, not just route between fixed steps.
slide6.body: Most systems marketed as "AI agents" are actually Level 3 or 4 — fixed chains or routers that branch between human-defined steps. The autonomy threshold is crossed only when the LLM itself controls the loop: deciding to retry, to revise, to call a different tool. Below the line, traditional governance still works. Above it, you need new security, observability, and approval gates.
slide6.levelsHumanBody: Code, LLM calls, chains, and routers. Every step is human-defined. Traditional governance (RBAC, audit logs, code review) is sufficient. Most "AI agents" sold today live here.
slide6.levelsLLMBody: State machines and autonomous goal-seekers. The LLM decides when to loop, retry, or switch strategy. Requires new security (runtime policy enforcement), observability (action replay), and approval gates (human-in-the-loop at high tiers).
slide6.cuscoPinBody: — it loops the perceive-reason-act cycle autonomously, with a circuit breaker for safety.

slide7.title: AI agents sit at the Peak of Inflated Expectations — the most aggressive adoption curve of any emerging technology measured.
slide7.body: The Gartner Hype Cycle tracks technology adoption through five phases. In the 2025 cycle, AI agents and AI-ready data are the two fastest-advancing technologies measured. The 2026 CIO Survey adds the adoption curve: 17% deployed today, 60% expect to deploy within two years. The window to learn the pattern is now — before your peers do.
slide7.chartBody: AI agents and AI-ready data are the two fastest-advancing technologies on the 2025 Gartner Hype Cycle. Generative AI has slid into the Trough of Disillusionment as organizations confront ROI reality ($1.9M avg spend per initiative, <30% CEO satisfaction).

slide8.title: 85% of employees are stuck at stages 2–3 of AI adoption — only 10% have reached the agentic stage.
slide8.body: BCG's adoption study maps employee AI usage across five stages. The damning finding: most organizations have purchased AI tools but haven't redesigned work around them. The gap between deployment and value is a process-redesign problem. Traditional camera systems (Stage 1-2) count people and trigger static alerts. ML/DL systems (Stage 2-3) detect graffiti, abandoned objects, fire, and slip hazards. But only agentic systems (Stage 4) close the loop — perceiving, reasoning, acting, and self-correcting with auto-generated reports and LLM-judged escalation. Only 25% have moved 40%+ of pilots to production.
slide8.bracket: 85% of employees stuck here — purchased tools, no process redesign

slide9.title: Vision Agent is built natively on Stage 4 — every plaza camera is a perceive-reason-act loop, not just a detector.
slide9.body: Most civic-camera systems are Stage 2: they count people and trigger a static threshold alert. Vision Agent closes the loop. The diagram below maps the canonical agentic loop onto the actual prototype components. The system handles crowd surge detection, graffiti and vandalism alerts, fire and smoke early warning, abandoned object detection, and post-earthquake structural damage assessment — all through the same perceive-reason-act-reflect pipeline with human feedback for governance.
slide9.analyticsBody: TF.js COCO-SSD detects persons. A 2-minute sliding-window z-score + EMA computes the anomaly score. Pure perception + statistics — no decisions.
slide9.agenticBody: Rule engine decides tier. LLM-as-judge filters false positives. Tool registry executes actions. Circuit breaker (max 5 escalations/hour) prevents runaway. The loop runs at 1 Hz, autonomously.
slide9.proofBody: When a crowd surge is detected, the system doesn't just beep — it captures a snapshot, sends an email, invokes the LLM judge, and auto-generates a corporate incident report. End-to-end, <2 seconds.

slide10.title: The window to learn the agentic pattern is now — before 60% of your peers deploy it in the next 24 months.
slide10.body: Agentic AI is not a future technology. It is a present-tense capability that most organizations will adopt within 24 months. The competitive question is not whether to deploy, but whether your governance, observability, and process redesign will be ready when you do.
slide10.quote: Agentic AI shifts human value beyond old-school productivity. AI can do that work instantly. Roles need to evolve.
slide10.quoteAttribution: — World Economic Forum, Rebuild the Enterprise for the Age of Agentic AI (2025)
slide10.action1Body: Pick a real sensor or data stream (camera, log, queue). Build the full loop — not just detection. Measure decision-to-action latency.
slide10.action2Body: Circuit breakers, audit trails, human-ack gates, runtime policy enforcement. Add these BEFORE the agent runs in production, not after.
slide10.action3Title: Treat the agent as a teammate
slide10.action3Body: Redesign the human role around supervision, not execution. The Deloitte gap (71% use, 25% scale) is a process-redesign problem.

Stages.stage1Def: Humans encode rules; the system executes deterministic logic. Every decision step is fully auditable because a human wrote each rule.
Stages.stage1Can2: Execute deterministic logic at machine speed
Stages.stage1Cant2: Learn from data — every edge case needs a new rule
Stages.stage1Value: Scalable automation of high-volume, well-bounded tasks. The assembly line of the digital age.
Stages.stage2Def: Models learn patterns directly from data. No human writes the rules — the model discovers them by minimizing error on a training set.
Stages.stage2Can1: Perceive — classify images, transcribe speech, rank results
Stages.stage2Can2: Detect anomalies and score risk at scale
Stages.stage2Can3: Improve as more data arrives (up to retraining)
Stages.stage2Cant1: Reason about goals or pursue multi-step objectives
Stages.stage2Cant3: Explain why it decided (opaque feature space)
Stages.stage2Value: Perception at scale. Image recognition, fraud scoring, recommendation engines — the entire 2010s AI economy.
Stages.stage3Def: Models trained on internet-scale data that synthesize new content — text, code, images, audio — by learning relationships across massive datasets.
Stages.stage3Cant1: Take action in the world — it waits for a prompt
Stages.stage3Cant2: Pursue a goal over time or across sessions
Stages.stage3Value: $33.9B private investment in 2024 (+18.7% YoY). 78% of organizations now use AI (up from 55%).
Stages.stage4Def: Systems that perceive, reason, act, and self-correct in a loop until a goal is met. They plan multi-step workflows, use tools, and revise course as conditions change.
Stages.stage4Can1: Plan multi-step workflows and revise plans
Stages.stage4Can2: Use tools and APIs autonomously (function calling)
Stages.stage4Can3: Reflect on errors and retry with a new strategy
Stages.stage4Cant1: Operate safely without governance and audit controls
Stages.stage4Cant2: Replace human judgment at high-stakes decision tiers
Stages.stage4Value: End-to-end process execution. "Sell work, not software" — targets the services profit pool, not the software profit pool.
